q: Dimethyl ether donates a lone pair to BF<sub>3</sub> to form the Lewis acid–base adduct (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>O–BF<sub>3</sub>. In this adduct every second-row atom has an octet. What are the formal charges on O and B?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons). Count bonds and lone pairs on each atom after the new O–B bond forms.
w: Oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. Boron has four bonds and no lone pairs: 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. The adduct is neutral overall, so the two charges must cancel. The donor atom (O) always becomes more positive and the acceptor (B) more negative when a dative bond forms.
x: This reverses the electron flow. O gave away a share of its lone pair, so it loses electron density and becomes +1; B gains a share and becomes −1.
Before the reaction both atoms are 0, but forming a fourth bond to B and a third bond to O changes the electron count on each.
The adduct is neutral, so a +1 on O must be balanced by a −1 somewhere. Boron with four bonds and no lone pairs is 3 − 4 = −1.

q: What is the hybridization of the tagged carbons a, b and c?
h: Count the σ-bonded neighbors (steric number) of each carbon. Two π bonds on one carbon leave it with two σ bonds.
w: Carbon a is the central carbon of an allene (C=C=C): it makes two σ bonds and two π bonds, so it is sp (linear). Carbon b has three σ bonds (to a, H and c) and one π bond, so it is sp2. Carbon c is a nitrile carbon with two σ bonds and two π bonds, so it is sp. A good shortcut: hybridization depends on the number of σ bonds plus lone pairs, not on how many double bonds you see in the drawing.
x: Carbon a has two double bonds, which means only two σ bonds; two σ domains give sp, not sp2.
Carbon b has three σ bonds (C, H, C) and only one π bond, so it is sp2; it is not part of two π bonds.
Carbon b is part of a C=C double bond, so it cannot be sp3, and the C≡N carbon has two π bonds, so it is sp.

q: Which statement correctly describes the three-dimensional shape of penta-2,3-diene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=C=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
c: The H–C–CH<sub>3</sub> plane at one end is perpendicular to the H–C–CH<sub>3</sub> plane at the other end
All five carbons and both alkene hydrogens lie in a single plane, as in a conjugated diene
The central carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, so the C=C=C bond angle is about 120°
The two π bonds use parallel p orbitals and are conjugated with each other
h: The central carbon uses one p orbital for each π bond. How are those two p orbitals oriented relative to each other?
w: The central allene carbon is sp with two unhybridized p orbitals at 90° to each other. One p orbital makes the π bond to C2, the other makes the π bond to C4. Each terminal carbon's p orbital must line up with one of them, so the substituent planes at the two ends are twisted 90° apart: the two H–C–CH3 planes are perpendicular. The C=C=C unit is linear (180°), and because the π bonds are orthogonal they are cumulated, not conjugated.
x: A planar arrangement would require both π bonds to use parallel p orbitals on the central carbon, but one carbon has no two parallel p orbitals; the ends are twisted 90°.
The central carbon has only two σ bonds, so it is sp and the C=C=C angle is 180°, not 120°.
The two π bonds are perpendicular, so they cannot overlap; cumulated double bonds are not conjugated.

q: Which species has a trigonal pyramidal geometry at the central atom?
h: Count electron domains (bonds plus lone pairs) on the central atom, then name the shape from the atoms only.
w: Trimethylamine has three σ bonds and one lone pair on N: four electron domains (tetrahedral electron geometry), but with only three atoms attached the shape is trigonal pyramidal. Trimethylborane has three bonds and no lone pair (trigonal planar), the tetramethylammonium ion has four bonds (tetrahedral), and the iminium N has three σ bonds plus a π bond (trigonal planar).
x: Boron in B(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> has only three bonding domains and no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar with an empty p orbital.
N in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>N<sup>+</sup> has four bonds and no lone pair, so the shape is tetrahedral, not pyramidal.
The iminium N has three σ bonds and one π bond and no lone pair, so it is sp<sup>2</sup> and trigonal planar.

q: In which species is the tagged carbon a sp2 hybridized with an empty unhybridized p orbital?
h: An empty p orbital means the carbon has fewer than eight electrons around it.
w: The tert-butyl cation has three σ bonds and only six valence electrons at the cationic carbon. It is sp2 and trigonal planar, and the leftover p orbital is empty; this is the LUMO that nucleophiles attack. The alkene carbon is also sp2, but its p orbital holds the π electrons.
x: The carbanion carbon has a lone pair, so its orbitals are all filled; a simple alkyl carbanion is roughly sp<sup>3</sup> and pyramidal.
This carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, but its p orbital is used for the C=C π bond, so it is filled, not empty.
The C–H carbon of isobutane has four σ bonds; it is sp<sup>3</sup> and has no unhybridized p orbital.

q: Which molecule has the smallest H–X–H bond angle at its central atom X?
h: Lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs and squeeze the bond angles.
w: Water has two lone pairs on an sp3-like oxygen; they push the O–H bonds together to about 104.5°. Ammonia has one lone pair (about 107°), methane none (109.5°), and formaldehyde has an sp2 carbon with an H–C–H angle near 116–120°.
x: NH<sub>3</sub> has only one lone pair, so its H–N–H angle (about 107°) is larger than water's.
CH<sub>4</sub> has no lone pairs, so it keeps the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.
The carbon in H<sub>2</sub>C=O is sp<sup>2</sup>, so its H–C–H angle is near 120°, the largest of the four.

q: How many σ bonds and how many π bonds are in acrylonitrile, shown below?
h: Every bond between two atoms has one σ bond; each extra line in a double or triple bond is a π bond. Count the hydrogens hidden in a line drawing.
w: Acrylonitrile is H2C=CH–C≡N (C3H3N). σ bonds: three C–H, the C=C, the C–C and the C≡N give 6 σ. π bonds: one in C=C and two in C≡N give 3 π.
x: The C≡N triple bond contains two π bonds, not one; together with the C=C that makes three.
This misses one of the three C–H bonds that a line drawing does not show.
A triple bond is one σ plus two π, not three σ bonds; multiple bonds add only one σ each.

q: Each tagged nitrogen has one lone pair. Which nitrogen(s) hold that lone pair in an sp2 hybrid orbital?
h: First decide each N's hybridization. Then ask whether the lone pair can sit in an unhybridized p orbital and overlap with a neighboring π bond.
w: Nitrogen a is an imine N: one σ bond to each carbon, a π bond, and a lone pair. The p orbital is used by the C=N π bond, so the lone pair lies in the plane in an sp2 orbital. Nitrogen b is an amide N: it is also sp2 (trigonal planar), but its lone pair sits in the p orbital so it can overlap with the C=O π bond (amide resonance). Nitrogen c is an ordinary amine N, sp3, with the lone pair in an sp3 orbital. Only a fits.
x: The amide N is sp<sup>2</sup>, but its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O π system, which requires a p orbital, not an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital.
Nitrogen a also qualifies, and b's lone pair is in a p orbital, not an sp2 orbital.
Nitrogen c is an amine with no adjacent π bond; it is sp3, and b's lone pair is in a p orbital.

q: The σ bond between carbons a and b in but-1-en-3-yne is formed by overlap of which orbitals?
h: Determine the hybridization of each carbon from the multiple bonds it is part of; the single bond between them uses one hybrid orbital from each.
w: Carbon a is part of the C=C double bond, so it is sp2. Carbon b is part of the C≡C triple bond, so it is sp. The single bond between them is a σ bond made from an sp2 orbital on a and an sp orbital on b. Because both orbitals have high s character, this C–C bond (about 1.43 Å) is shorter than the sp3–sp3 bond in ethane (1.54 Å).
x: Carbon b is part of a triple bond and has only two σ bonds, so it uses sp, not sp2, orbitals.
Carbon a is in the double bond, not the triple bond, so it is sp2.
Carbon a has a π bond, so it cannot be sp3.

q:
Consider each species drawn with all second-row atoms obeying the octet rule.
I. In BH4−, boron has a formal charge of −1.
II. In (CH3)3O+, oxygen has a formal charge of +1.
III. In carbon monoxide (C≡O), carbon has a formal charge of 0.
Which statements are true?
h: Apply valence − nonbonding − ½ bonding to each atom. For C≡O, count the lone pair on carbon.
w: I: B has 4 bonds, no lone pairs: 3 − 0 − 4 = −1 (true). II: O has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1 (true). III: in :C≡O:, carbon has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, and O is +1, so III is false. Answer: I and II only. The carbon of CO bears the negative formal charge even though O is more electronegative, which is why CO binds metals through carbon.
x: Statement II is also true: an oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair is +1, just like hydronium.
Statement III is false: the octet structure of CO puts −1 on carbon and +1 on oxygen.
Statement III is false; C in :C≡O: is 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, not 0.

q: In which compound is the lone pair on the tagged nitrogen a delocalized by resonance?
h: A lone pair is delocalized only if its atom is directly attached to a π bond (or an empty p orbital). An sp<sup>3</sup> carbon in between breaks the connection.
w: In N-methylacetamide the nitrogen is bonded directly to the carbonyl carbon, so its lone pair overlaps with the C=O π bond (a second resonance form puts C=N+ and O−). In allylamine, benzylamine and 4-aminobutan-2-one there is at least one sp3 CH2 between N and the π system, so the lone pair is localized and the N is a normal sp3 amine.
x: In allylamine the N is attached to an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>, not to the alkene carbon; the lone pair cannot overlap with the C=C π bond (only an N on the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, as in an enamine, would be conjugated).
Benzylamine's N sits on a CH<sub>2</sub> next to the ring, so the lone pair is not conjugated with the aromatic π system; that is why benzylamine is about as basic as an alkylamine.
The C=O is two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons away from N, so the lone pair is localized; there is no resonance form moving it toward oxygen.

q: In the best Lewis structure of methyl isocyanate (shown), how many lone pairs are there in total, and what is the hybridization of the carbon bonded to both N and O?
h: Give N and O octets with the double bonds shown, then count σ bonds on the N=C=O carbon.
w: With CH3–N=C=O and no formal charges, N (two bonds) has one lone pair and O (one double bond) has two lone pairs: 3 lone pairs. The N=C=O carbon makes two σ bonds and two π bonds, so it is sp and the N=C=O unit is linear, like CO2.
x: The central carbon has two double bonds and therefore only two σ bonds; two σ domains make it sp, not sp<sup>2</sup>.
N with two bonds needs only one lone pair to complete its octet; giving it two would make it −1.
Oxygen with one double bond needs two lone pairs, and the N=C=O carbon is sp because it has only two σ bonds.

q: In N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) the two N–CH3 groups give separate 1H NMR signals at 25 °C because rotation about the C–N bond is slow (barrier about 85 kJ/mol). What is the best explanation for this large barrier?
c: Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character; rotation breaks the N lone pair’s overlap with C=O
Steric clash between the N-methyl groups and the carbonyl oxygen locks the molecule in one fixed conformation
Hydrogen bonds from the N-methyl hydrogens to the carbonyl oxygen hold the methyl groups in place
The nitrogen is sp<sup>3</sup>, and slow pyramidal inversion at N keeps the methyl groups apart
h: Draw the second resonance contributor of an amide. What kind of bond does it show between C and N?
w: An amide has a contributor with C=N+ and O−. In the hybrid the N is sp2 and planar and its lone pair (in a p orbital) overlaps with the C=O π bond, so the C–N bond has partial double-bond character. Rotating 90° about that bond would twist the N p orbital out of alignment and destroy the delocalization, which costs much more energy than rotating about an ordinary single bond (about 12 kJ/mol). The two methyl groups are therefore locked cis and trans to O on the NMR time scale.
x: Steric strain from small methyl groups is only a few kJ/mol; it cannot account for a barrier near 85 kJ/mol.
C–H bonds of methyl groups are not hydrogen-bond donors; H bonding requires H on N, O or F.
Amide nitrogens are sp<sup>2</sup> and planar, not sp<sup>3</sup>; N inversion is fast and would not separate the methyl signals anyway.

q: Which compound has no net molecular dipole moment?
h: Add the C–Cl bond dipoles as vectors. Do any two point in exactly opposite directions?
w: In trans-1,2-dichloroethene the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions across a center of symmetry and cancel, so μ = 0. In the cis isomer and in 1,1-dichloroethene both C–Cl dipoles point toward the same side, and in CH2Cl2 the tetrahedral arrangement leaves a net dipole.
x: In the cis isomer both chlorines are on the same side of the double bond, so their bond dipoles add to a net dipole.
Both C–Cl bonds in 1,1-dichloroethene point away from the same carbon at about 120°; they partly reinforce, giving a net dipole.
In tetrahedral CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> the two C–Cl dipoles are about 110° apart and do not cancel.

q: In which molecule do all of the atoms lie in one plane?
h: Any sp<sup>3</sup> carbon has hydrogens out of the plane. In allene, think about the two perpendicular π bonds.
w: In acrylonitrile every atom is sp2 or sp: the vinyl group is planar and the C–C≡N unit is linear and lies in that plane, so all seven atoms are coplanar. Propene and acetaldehyde contain a CH3 group whose tetrahedral hydrogens cannot all lie in the plane. In allene the two CH2 groups are twisted 90° from each other.
x: Allene's two π bonds are perpendicular, so the H–C–H plane at one end is perpendicular to the one at the other end.
The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon of propene is sp<sup>3</sup>; at most one of its hydrogens can lie in the plane of the alkene.
The methyl group of acetaldehyde is sp<sup>3</sup>, so two of its hydrogens sit above and below the plane of the C=O group.

q: Starting from N-methylacetamide as drawn, one curved arrow is drawn from the nitrogen lone pair to the C–N bond, and a second arrow from the C=O π bond onto oxygen. What are the formal charges on N and O in the new resonance contributor?
h: Follow the electrons: which atom loses a share of a lone pair, and which atom gains a lone pair?
w: The first arrow turns the N lone pair into a C=N π bond, so N goes from three bonds + one lone pair (0) to four bonds and no lone pair: +1. The second arrow moves the C=O π electrons onto oxygen, giving O one bond and three lone pairs: −1. Carbon keeps four bonds and stays neutral, and the contributor stays neutral overall.
x: The arrows move electron density away from N and toward O, so N becomes positive and O negative, not the reverse.
That pattern (C<sup>+</sup>, O<sup>−</sup>) would come from the C=O arrow alone; the N lone-pair arrow gives carbon a new bond, so carbon stays neutral and N becomes +1.
Oxygen gains the π electrons as a third lone pair, so it must become −1; a net +1 charge would also make the neutral amide charged.

q: A nucleophile adds to formaldehyde at carbon, while a proton or Lewis acid binds at oxygen. Which molecular-orbital description best explains this pattern?
c: The nucleophile donates into the π*<sub>C=O</sub> LUMO, which is larger on carbon; the acid accepts a nonbonding lone pair on oxygen
The nucleophile donates into the π<sub>C=O</sub> bonding orbital, which is concentrated on carbon; the acid accepts the π* electrons on oxygen
The nucleophile donates into the σ*<sub>C–H</sub> orbital, and the acid accepts the C=O π bonding electrons
The nucleophile donates into the π*<sub>C=O</sub> LUMO, which is larger on oxygen; the acid binds the lone pair on carbon
h: Nucleophiles fill an empty orbital (a LUMO); acids take electrons from a filled one. Where is each orbital concentrated in a polar C=O?
w: Formaldehyde's LUMO is π*C=O. Because O is more electronegative, the bonding π orbital is concentrated on O and the antibonding π* has its larger lobe on carbon, so nucleophiles attack C (roughly 107° from the C=O axis). The highest filled orbitals are the nonbonding lone pairs on oxygen, so protons and Lewis acids bind at O.
x: The π bonding orbital is already full and is larger on oxygen; a nucleophile must add electrons to an empty orbital.
σ*<sub>C–H</sub> is high in energy and attack there would be an S<sub>N</sub>2-like hydride displacement, which does not happen; acids bind the oxygen lone pairs.
In a polar π bond the antibonding orbital is larger on the less electronegative atom (carbon), and carbon in formaldehyde has no lone pair.
